title: Chest Mark Fundamentals
primarySkill: Executing a secure two-handed chest mark
objective: Establish the fundamental technique required to track, receive and secure a football arriving between waist and chest height.
groundSize: Pairs operate approximately five to eight metres apart within clearly marked lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 1 – Introductory technical instruction
setup:
- Organise players into pairs.
- Position partners five metres apart for junior or foundation players.
- More experienced players may begin seven to eight metres apart.
- One player acts as the feeder and the other as the marker.
- The feeder uses a controlled two-handed throw or short kick that arrives between the receiver’s waist and chest.
- Each pair operates inside a separate lane.
- Demonstrate the correct hand shape and cushioning action before beginning.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The marker stands in a balanced position with the feet approximately shoulder-width apart.
2. The feeder delivers the football towards the centre of the marker’s body.
3. The marker tracks the football from the feeder’s hands or foot.
4. Both hands extend towards the football with fingers spread and thumbs positioned behind it.
5. The football is contacted in front of the body.
6. The elbows bend to cushion the football towards the chest.
7. The marker secures the football firmly with two hands.
8. The football is returned to the feeder.
9. Complete eight to ten repetitions before changing roles.
10. Repeat with the football delivered slightly left and right while remaining within one step of the marker.
coachingPoints: - Keep the eyes on the football until it is fully secured.
- Move the hands towards the football rather than waiting for it to strike the chest.
- Spread the fingers to create a large, strong catching surface.
- Position the thumbs behind the football.
- Contact the football in front of the body.
- Cushion the football by bending the elbows.
- Bring the football securely to the chest after contact.
- Maintain a balanced stance throughout the mark.
- Communicate with a clear call before the football arrives.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
- Whether players track the football continuously.
- Whether both hands move towards the football.
- Whether fingers are spread and thumbs remain behind the football.
- Whether the football is contacted in front of the body.
- Whether the elbows cushion the impact.
- Whether the football is secured before the player relaxes.
- Whether players remain balanced during the mark.
progressions: - Use short controlled kicks instead of throws.
- Deliver the football slightly left or right.
- Require the marker to call before every delivery.
- Complete consecutive marks without dropping the football.
regressions: - Use a smaller or softer football.
- Deliver with a gentle two-handed throw.
- Keep every delivery directly in front of the player.
- Allow the player to begin with hands already extended.
successIndicators: - Track the football into the hands.
- Contact the football in front of the body.
matchApplication: The chest mark is used when a kick arrives between waist and chest height and the player has time to meet the football with two hands. Secure technique prevents rebounds and allows the player to prepare the next disposal quickly.

title: Overhead Mark Fundamentals
primarySkill: Executing a secure two-handed overhead mark
objective: Establish the correct hand position, arm extension and cushioning technique required to mark a football above head height.
groundSize: Pairs operate five to eight metres apart within marked lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic overhead technique instruction
setup:
- Organise players into pairs.
- Position partners five to eight metres apart.
- One player acts as the feeder and the other as the marker.
- The feeder uses a controlled lob or short kick that arrives slightly above the marker’s head.
- Players remain stationary during the introductory repetitions.
- Demonstrate hand position with fingers spread and thumbs forming a strong base behind the football.
- Ensure sufficient space between pairs for raised arms and football flight.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The marker begins in a balanced stance with the eyes on the feeder.
2. The feeder delivers the football slightly above the marker’s head.
3. The marker tracks the football and raises both hands early.
4. The arms extend upwards and slightly forwards.
5. The football is contacted above eye level with fingers spread.
6. The thumbs remain behind the football to prevent it passing through the hands.
7. The elbows bend after contact to cushion the football down.
8. The player brings the football securely towards the chest.
9. Complete eight repetitions before changing roles.
10. Repeat with the football delivered slightly to either side of the marker.
coachingPoints: - Track the football from release to completion.
- Raise the hands early enough to establish position.
- Extend towards the football rather than allowing it to descend onto the head.
- Keep the fingers spread and relaxed.
- Position both thumbs behind the football.
- Contact the football above eye level where possible.
- Cushion the football by bending the elbows after contact.
- Bring the football down securely with two hands.
- Maintain a stable base beneath the marking point.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
- Whether the player tracks the football without turning away.
- Whether the hands rise early.
- Whether the arms extend towards the football.
- Whether the football is contacted above eye level.
- Whether the thumbs prevent the football passing through.
- Whether the player cushions and secures the mark.
- Whether balance is maintained beneath the football.
progressions: - Increase the height of the delivery.
- Use controlled kicks instead of lobbed throws.
- Require one adjustment step before marking.
- Add a small vertical jump for suitable players.
regressions: - Use a softer or junior football.
- Allow the player to begin with hands raised.
- Practise hand position with a stationary football before feeding.
successIndicators: - Use both thumbs behind the football.
matchApplication: The overhead mark is used when a kick arrives above head height and the player can reach the football before it drops into a more contested position. Taking the football high reduces interception opportunities and provides stronger control.

title: Low Mark Fundamentals
primarySkill: Executing a secure two-handed mark below waist height
objective: Establish the technique required to lower the body, place the hands correctly and secure a football arriving below waist height.
groundSize: Pairs operate five to seven metres apart in marked lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic low-mark technique instruction
setup:
- Organise players into pairs.
- Position partners five to seven metres apart.
- One player acts as the feeder and the other as the marker.
- The feeder delivers a controlled football between ankle and waist height.
- Deliveries should remain within one step of the marker.
- Players alternate between low straight, low left and low right deliveries.
- Ensure the surface is clear and safe for bending and low movement.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The marker begins in a balanced ready position.
2. The feeder delivers the football below waist height.
3. The marker tracks the flight and moves the feet behind the football.
4. The knees and hips bend to lower the body.
5. Both hands reach towards the football with fingers pointing down or slightly forwards.
6. The football is contacted in front of the legs.
7. The elbows and hands cushion the football into the body.
8. The player rises while securing possession with two hands.
9. Complete six straight deliveries and four to either side.
10. Change roles and repeat.
coachingPoints: - Move the feet to place the body behind the football.
- Bend through the knees and hips rather than folding only at the waist.
- Keep the head and eyes above the football where possible.
- Present both hands early.
- Point the fingers down for a low football.
- Contact the football in front of the legs.
- Cushion and secure the football before standing upright.
- Be prepared to continue into a ground-ball collection if the mark is not completed.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
- Whether the player moves behind the football.
- Whether the knees and hips flex.
- Whether the head remains stable.
- Whether both hands reach low and forward.
- Whether the football is contacted before it reaches the legs.
- Whether the player secures possession before standing.
- Whether balance is maintained on low side deliveries.
progressions: - Use short kicks instead of throws.
- Allow a live ground-ball continuation after a dropped mark.
regressions: - Deliver the football slowly by hand.
- Keep the football directly in front.
- Allow the player to begin in a lowered position.
successIndicators: - Position the body behind the football.
- Lower through the knees and hips.
- Present two hands below the football.
- Contact it in front of the legs.
- Remain prepared for a ground-ball recovery.
matchApplication: Low marks occur when a kick drops quickly or travels towards the player’s legs. Correct body positioning improves the chance of completing the mark and places the player in the best position to recover if the football spills.
relatedDrills: - HB-049 – Ground-Ball Win and Handball Exit

title: Cushion and Secure Marking
primarySkill: Absorbing the football cleanly and securing possession after initial contact
objective: Develop the cushioning and securing action required to prevent the football rebounding from the hands at different marking heights.
groundSize: Pairs operate approximately five to eight metres apart in separate lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic control and security observation
setup:
- Organise players into pairs.
- Position partners five to eight metres apart.
- The feeder delivers footballs at three controlled heights:
- Low.
- Chest.
- Overhead.
- The marker focuses on absorbing and securing rather than returning quickly.
- Place a security cone one metre behind the marker.
- After each mark, the player must maintain control while turning towards the security cone.
- Change roles after nine repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The feeder calls the delivery height immediately before releasing the football.
2. The marker adjusts the hands and body position.
3. The player meets the football in front or above the body.
4. The elbows bend immediately after contact.
5. The football is guided into a secure two-handed position.
6. The marker holds the football firmly against the body.
7. The player turns towards the security cone without losing possession.
8. The football is returned to the feeder.
9. Complete three marks at each height.
10. Change roles and repeat.
coachingPoints: - Meet the football rather than allowing it to strike the body.
- Keep the hands relaxed before contact and strong once the football arrives.
- Bend the elbows to absorb momentum.
- Bring the football into a secure position immediately.
- Use two hands to complete control.
- Do not relax after the first touch.
- Maintain possession while turning after the mark.
- Adjust the cushioning action to the speed of the delivery.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
- Whether the player meets the football.
- Whether the hands remain relaxed before contact.
- Whether the elbows cushion the delivery.
- Whether the football rebounds.
- Whether possession is secured with two hands.
- Whether the player maintains control while turning.
- Whether technique changes appropriately for each height.
progressions: - Vary the height without announcing it.
- Add a controlled turn to either side.
- Require the player to protect the football from a shadow opponent after marking.
regressions: - Practise one height at a time.
successIndicators: - Meet the football with the hands.
- Maintain control during the post-mark turn.
- Adapt the hand position to different heights.
matchApplication: A player must complete more than the initial contact to secure a mark. Cushioning and strong post-contact control reduce spills and prevent nearby opponents from dislodging the football.

title: Marking Footwork to the Football Line
primarySkill: Using adjustment footwork to position the body on the football’s line
objective: Develop the footwork required to move behind or beneath the football and complete the appropriate chest, overhead or low mark.
groundSize: Lanes approximately eight metres long and five metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate footwork and flight-reading observation
setup:
- Organise players into pairs.
- Mark a central starting cone for the marker.
- Place one adjustment cone one metre to the left and one to the right.
- Position the feeder six to eight metres away.
- The feeder delivers the football left, centre or right and at varied safe heights.
- The marker must move the feet and establish body position before marking.
- Deliveries should remain achievable within two or three adjustment steps.
- Change roles after nine repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The marker begins at the central cone in a balanced ready position.
2. The feeder delivers the football left, centre or right.
3. The marker tracks the football immediately.
4. The player uses short adjustment steps to move behind or beneath its line.
5. The body is aligned with the expected marking point.
6. The player selects the appropriate low, chest or overhead technique.
7. The football is marked and secured.
8. The marker returns to the central cone.
9. Complete three deliveries to each general area in an unpredictable order.
10. Change roles and repeat.
coachingPoints: - Read the football immediately after it leaves the feeder.
- Move the feet before reaching with the hands.
- Use short, balanced adjustment steps.
- Avoid crossing the feet when making small lateral corrections.
- Position the body behind the football where possible.
- Select the marking technique according to the height.
- Keep the head stable during the final steps.
- Arrive balanced rather than lunging at the football.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
- Whether players react early to the delivery.
- Whether footwork moves the body into line.
- Whether players reach without moving.
- Whether the final steps remain controlled.
- Whether the correct marking technique is selected.
- Whether the player contacts the football from balance.
- Whether the player returns promptly for the next repetition.
progressions: - Add a forward or backward adjustment.
- Require a quick post-mark turn towards a nominated side.
regressions: - Practise one marking height at a time.
- Allow the marker to begin closer to the expected line.
successIndicators: - Position the body on the football’s line.
matchApplication: Players rarely receive every kick directly at their body. Early flight recognition and efficient adjustment footwork allow them to complete more marks and reduce the number of footballs reaching ground level.

title: Three-Height Partner Marking Circuit
primarySkill: Selecting and executing the correct marking technique for varied football heights
objective: Integrate low, chest and overhead marking techniques within a controlled partner activity requiring the receiver to recognise and respond to varied deliveries.
groundSize: Pairs operate six to ten metres apart within marked lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate delivery control and technique selection
setup:
- Organise players into pairs.
- Position partners six metres apart for junior players and up to ten metres apart for experienced players.
- One player begins as the kicker or feeder.
- The marker remains inside a three-metre receiving zone.
- The feeder delivers footballs at low, chest and overhead heights.
- Deliveries should be unpredictable but safe and controllable.
- The marker returns the football after each completed mark.
- Change roles after twelve deliveries.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The feeder prepares a controlled delivery.
2. The marker watches the football from the moment of release.
3. The player identifies whether the expected mark is low, chest or overhead.
4. The marker adjusts the feet within the receiving zone.
5. The correct hand position is established.
6. The football is met and cushioned.
7. The marker secures possession with two hands.
8. The football is returned to the feeder.
9. Complete four deliveries at each height in an unpredictable sequence.
10. Change roles and repeat.
coachingPoints: - Read the football early enough to select the correct technique.
- Move the feet to support the hands.
- Use fingers down for low marks.
- Use thumbs behind the football for chest and overhead marks.
- Contact the football in front of the body or above eye level.
- Cushion every delivery.
- Secure possession before returning the football.
- Feeders must prioritise accuracy and appropriate challenge.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
- Whether players identify the delivery height early.
- Whether footwork supports the selected mark.
- Whether hand position changes appropriately.
- Whether players attempt the wrong technique.
- Whether the football is cushioned.
- Whether possession is secured.
- Whether feeders provide useful and safe deliveries.
progressions: - Require consecutive clean marks for scoring.
- Add a one-step movement outside the receiving zone.
- Nominate a post-mark direction after possession is secured.
regressions: - Practise one height for several repetitions.
successIndicators: - Complete clean marks across all three heights.
matchApplication: Kicks arrive at different heights and angles. Players who recognise flight early and select the appropriate technique are more likely to complete the mark rather than allowing the football to spill.
relatedDrills: - MK-005 – Marking Footwork to the Football Line

title: Straight-Lead Chest Mark
primarySkill: Timing a straight lead and completing a chest mark while moving forward
objective: Develop the ability to time a forward lead, present a clear target and complete a chest mark without stopping before the football arrives.
groundSize: Lanes approximately 15 metres long and five metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate lead and delivery timing
setup:
- Organise players into groups of three to five.
- Place the kicker at one end of the lane.
- The marker begins eight to ten metres away at a starting cone.
- Mark a receiving gate three to four metres in front of the marker.
- A third player waits behind the kicker or at the far end for rotation.
- The marker leads directly towards the kicker.
- The kicker aims to deliver the football between waist and chest height.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The kicker establishes possession and looks towards the marker.
2. The marker begins the lead and accelerates towards the receiving gate.
3. The marker calls and presents both hands.
4. The kicker delivers the football into the player’s forward path.
5. The marker tracks the football while continuing through the gate.
6. The player meets the football with both hands.
7. The elbows cushion the football towards the chest.
8. The marker secures possession and decelerates under control.
9. The marker carries the football back to the kicking line while the kicker becomes the next marker.
10. Continue the rotation and practise receiving from both right- and left-foot kickers where possible.
coachingPoints: - Begin the lead when the kicker is balanced and ready.
- Accelerate during the first steps.
- Run directly towards the kicker during the introductory version.
- Communicate early and present two hands.
- The kicker should place the football in front of the marker.
- The marker should not stop and wait beneath the football.
- Meet the football while moving.
- Secure possession before decelerating or turning.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
- Whether the lead begins at the correct time.
- Whether the marker accelerates.
- Whether the kicker sees and responds to the lead.
- Whether the football is placed in the running path.
- Whether the marker continues moving through the mark.
- Whether the football is cushioned and secured.
- Whether deceleration remains controlled.
progressions: - Move the receiving gate slightly left or right.
- Require the marker to play on after securing the football.
regressions: - Use a controlled throw instead of a kick.
- Slow the lead to a jog.
- Allow the marker to begin closer to the kicker.
successIndicators: - Time the lead from the kicker’s readiness.
matchApplication: A straight lead provides the ball carrier with a clear and predictable target. Marking while maintaining forward movement helps the receiver create separation and continue the next phase quickly.
relatedDrills: - MK-005 – Marking Footwork to the Football Line

title: Running Overhead Mark
primarySkill: Completing an overhead mark while moving towards the football
objective: Develop the ability to lead towards a higher kick, judge its flight and complete a secure overhead mark without losing running balance.
groundSize: Lanes approximately 18 metres long and six metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate flight and moving-overhead technique management
setup:
- Organise players into groups of three to five.
- Position the kicker at one end of the lane.
- The marker begins ten to twelve metres away.
- Mark a receiving zone four metres in front of the marker.
- The kicker delivers a controlled higher kick into the receiving zone.
- A third player waits as a rotation or return player.
- Ensure lanes are separated sufficiently for higher football flight.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The kicker establishes possession and signals readiness.
2. The marker begins a controlled forward lead.
3. The kicker delivers a higher football into the receiving zone.
4. The marker tracks the flight while adjusting running speed.
5. Both hands rise early.
6. The player moves beneath or slightly behind the dropping football.
7. The arms extend and the football is contacted above eye level.
8. The marker cushions and secures the football.
9. The player decelerates and returns the football for rotation.
10. Repeat with the receiving zone positioned slightly left and right.
coachingPoints: - Lead only when the kicker is prepared.
- Track the football immediately after the kick.
- Adjust running speed rather than continuing at one pace.
- Move beneath the expected drop point.
- Raise the hands early.
- Extend towards the football at the highest comfortable point.
- Keep the thumbs behind the football.
- Secure possession before lowering the hands or changing direction.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
- Whether the marker tracks the football early.
- Whether running speed changes according to flight.
- Whether the player reaches the correct drop point.
- Whether hands rise before the football arrives.
- Whether the football is contacted above eye level.
- Whether the player cushions and secures possession.
- Whether balance remains controlled after the mark.
progressions: - Add a small jump at the marking point.
- Require a controlled play-on after the mark.
regressions: - Allow the marker to begin with hands raised.
matchApplication: Higher kicks to a leading player require the receiver to judge both distance and drop. Taking the football overhead before it descends reduces the opportunity for a trailing opponent to spoil.
relatedDrills: - MK-005 – Marking Footwork to the Football Line

title: Mark, Secure and Protect
primarySkill: Securing the football after a mark and moving it into a protected position
objective: Develop the habit of completing the mark, securing the football with two hands and protecting it before preparing the next movement or disposal.
groundSize: Stations approximately ten metres long and eight metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate security and pressure-side observation
setup:
- Organise players into groups of three: feeder, marker and shadow-pressure player.
- The feeder stands six to eight metres from the marker.
- The pressure player begins two metres behind or to one side of the marker.
- The feeder delivers a controlled chest or overhead football.
- The pressure player may approach after the mark but may not spoil or tackle.
- Mark one protection gate to the left and one to the right.
- Rotate roles after four repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The feeder delivers the football to the marker.
2. The marker tracks, meets and secures the football.
3. The pressure player approaches from the nominated side after possession is completed.
4. The marker identifies the pressure direction.
5. The football is moved firmly to the side away from the pressure.
6. The player turns the feet and body towards the opposite protection gate.
7. The marker carries the football through the gate under control.
8. The pressure player follows without making contact.
9. Reset and change the pressure side.
10. Rotate all roles.
coachingPoints: - Complete the mark before preparing the next action.
- Maintain two-hand control immediately after contact.
- Scan or listen for approaching pressure.
- Move the football to the protected side.
- Turn the feet rather than twisting only through the upper body.
- Keep the football close to the torso.
- Maintain balance through the turn.
- Do not play on automatically if the pressure relationship is unclear.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
- Whether the mark is completed before the turn begins.
- Whether two-hand control is maintained.
- Whether the pressure side is recognised.
- Whether the football moves away from the opponent.
- Whether the feet reposition during the turn.
- Whether the player remains balanced.
- Whether the pressure player waits until the mark is completed.
progressions: - Allow the pressure player to choose the approach side.
- Increase the speed of the approach.
- Add a controlled handball after entering the protection gate.
- Add a passive spoil attempt before the mark.
- Require the marker to decide whether to hold or play on.
matchApplication: Completing the mark does not end the pressure situation. Players must secure and protect the football immediately, particularly when an opponent is arriving from behind or one side.
relatedDrills: - MK-005 – Marking Footwork to the Football Line

title: Fundamental Marking Competency Assessment
primarySkill: Assessing fundamental marking technique across varied heights and basic movement
objective: Assess each player’s ability to track, position, mark and secure the football using fundamental chest, overhead and low marking techniques.
groundSize: Five assessment stations arranged within an area approximately 35 metres × 25 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced technical assessment and feedback management
setup:
- Establish five assessment stations:
- Station 1: Stationary chest marking.
- Station 2: Stationary overhead marking.
- Station 3: Low marking.
- Station 4: Footwork to varied delivery lines.
- Station 5: Straight lead and moving mark.
- Divide players evenly between stations.
- Assign a coach or trained observer to each station where possible.
- Use consistent delivery distances and target areas.
- Allow one practice repetition before formal assessment.
- Record technique, completion and ball-security outcomes separately.
- Adjust delivery speed appropriately for age and skill level.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. At Station 1, each player completes five chest-mark attempts.
2. At Station 2, each player completes five overhead-mark attempts.
3. At Station 3, each player completes five low-mark attempts.
4. At Station 4, each player completes six marks requiring left, right and forward footwork adjustments.
5. At Station 5, each player completes four straight-leading marks.
6. Observers score tracking, footwork, hand position, cushioning and security.
7. Players rotate after all group members complete the required attempts.
8. Missed marks are recorded with the primary cause.
9. Each player receives one technical strength and one priority correction.
10. Players repeat the station linked to their lowest technical score.
coachingPoints: - Apply consistent standards across all players.
- Assess football tracking from the moment of delivery.
- Record whether the feet support the marking attempt.
- Judge the correctness of hand position for each height.
- Observe whether the football is met rather than trapped.
- Include cushioning and post-contact security.
- Distinguish a poor delivery from a technical marking error.
- Assess moving marks by whether the player maintains momentum and balance.
- Provide feedback linked to one observable action.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
- Whether the player tracks the football continuously.
- Whether hand position matches the delivery height.
- Whether footwork places the body on the football’s line.
- Whether contact occurs in front or at the highest comfortable point.
- Whether the elbows cushion the football.
- Whether possession is secured with two hands.
- Whether leading players time movement correctly.
- Whether feedback is applied during the repeated station.
progressions: - Repeat the assessment later and compare results.
successIndicators: - Complete chest, overhead and low marks.
matchApplication: Reliable marking begins with strong fundamental technique. This assessment identifies whether players can select and execute the correct mark before progressing to more demanding movement, contested and tactical marking activities.
relatedDrills: - MK-005 – Marking Footwork to the Football Line

title: One-Grab Marking Control
primarySkill: Securing the football cleanly with one controlled marking action
objective: Develop clean first-contact control so the football is secured without juggling, double-grabbing or trapping it against the body.
groundSize: Pairs operate six to ten metres apart within marked lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic first-contact control observation
setup:
Organise players into pairs.
Position partners six metres apart for developing players and up to ten metres apart for experienced groups.
One player begins as the feeder and the other as the marker.
The feeder delivers controlled footballs at chest height.
Markers score only when the football is secured with one clean contact.
Juggled, trapped or rebounding marks do not count.
Change roles after ten deliveries.
Keep all deliveries within one adjustment step during the first round.
howTheDrillWorks:
The marker begins in a balanced ready position.
The feeder delivers the football towards the marker’s chest.
The marker tracks the football continuously.
Both hands extend towards the football.
The fingers spread and the thumbs remain behind the football.
The marker meets and cushions the football.
The football is secured immediately without a second grab.
The marker holds possession for two seconds to confirm control.
The football is returned to the feeder.
Complete ten repetitions before changing roles.
coachingPoints: Track the football until possession is fully secured.
Meet the football with two hands.
Keep the hands relaxed before contact.
Apply firm finger pressure at the moment of contact.
Bend the elbows to absorb the football.
Avoid relying on the chest to stop the ball.
Maintain two-hand control after the mark.
Judge success by clean first contact, not merely eventual possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the player tracks the football fully.
Whether both hands meet the football together.
Whether the fingers and thumbs create a secure shape.
Whether the elbows cushion the delivery.
Whether the football rebounds or is juggled.
Whether the body remains balanced.
Whether the player holds possession after the mark.
progressions: Use short kicks rather than hand feeds.
Include chest, low and overhead one-grab marks.
regressions: Use a smaller or softer football.
Deliver directly to the centre of the body.
Allow the player to begin with hands extended.
successIndicators: Track the football into the hands.
Avoid trapping it against the chest.
matchApplication: A one-grab mark allows the player to secure possession before an opponent can spoil, tackle or recover. Clean first contact also enables faster preparation for the next disposal.

title: Extended-Arms Chest Mark
primarySkill: Marking the football with fully presented arms in front of the body
objective: Develop the ability to meet the football well in front of the torso, reducing the chance of body contact, rebounds and late defensive spoils.
groundSize: Pairs operate six to ten metres apart within five-metre-wide lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic hand-presentation and reach correction
setup:
Organise players into pairs.
Position partners six to ten metres apart.
One player feeds and one marks.
Place a flat marker approximately half a metre in front of the marker’s starting position.
The marker must contact the football above or in front of the marker rather than allowing it to reach the torso.
Begin with controlled chest-height hand feeds.
Change roles after eight to ten repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The marker begins with the hands relaxed near the torso.
The feeder delivers the football towards chest height.
The marker raises and extends both arms early.
The hands move beyond the front reach marker.
The football is contacted with fingers spread and thumbs behind.
The elbows bend immediately after contact.
The football is cushioned towards the body.
The marker secures possession with two hands.
The football is returned to the feeder.
Repeat before changing roles.
coachingPoints: Raise the hands before the football reaches the body.
Extend towards the football without locking the elbows.
Meet the football as far in front as balance allows.
Keep the head and chest behind the hands.
Spread the fingers and maintain strong thumb support.
Cushion after contact rather than pulling the hands backwards early.
Secure the football before lowering the hands.
Maintain a balanced stance throughout.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the hands are presented early.
Whether contact occurs in front of the body.
Whether the elbows remain slightly flexed.
Whether the player reaches without losing balance.
Whether the football is cushioned.
Whether possession is secured cleanly.
Whether players revert to body trapping as delivery speed increases.
progressions: Require the marker to move one step towards the football.
Score only marks taken beyond the reach marker.
regressions: Allow the player to begin with hands extended.
successIndicators: Meet the football well in front.
matchApplication: Taking the football in front increases control and reduces the time available for a trailing opponent to spoil. It also keeps the player’s body between the football and pressure.

title: Thumb-Position Marking Control
primarySkill: Maintaining correct thumb position behind the football during chest and overhead marks
objective: Reinforce the thumb and hand shape required to stop the football passing between or through the hands during chest-height and overhead marking.
groundSize: Pairs operate five to eight metres apart within marked lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic hand-shape instruction and correction
setup:
Organise players into pairs.
Demonstrate the correct chest-mark and overhead-mark hand shapes.
Position partners five to eight metres apart.
The feeder alternates chest-height and overhead deliveries.
Before each feed, the marker briefly shows the correct hand position.
The feeder waits until the hand shape is correct.
Change roles after twelve deliveries.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder calls “chest” or “overhead”.
The marker displays the matching hand position.
The feeder delivers the football at the nominated height.
The marker tracks the football and maintains the hand shape.
Both thumbs remain behind the football.
The fingers wrap securely around its sides.
The elbows cushion the football after contact.
The player secures possession with two hands.
Complete six chest and six overhead marks.
Change roles and repeat.
coachingPoints: Keep both thumbs behind the football.
Avoid allowing the thumbs to spread so widely that a central gap appears.
Keep fingers extended and ready before contact.
Wrap the fingers around the football as it arrives.
Use the same strong thumb base at chest and overhead height.
Maintain relaxed hands before contact.
Cushion after the football is stopped.
Continue looking at the football until it is secured.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the correct hand shape is shown before the feed.
Whether thumbs remain behind the football at contact.
Whether the hands separate too widely.
Whether fingers wrap around the football.
Whether the football passes through or rebounds.
Whether the player maintains the same technique overhead.
Whether both hands work together.
progressions: Complete consecutive marks without hand-position errors.
regressions: Practise hand shapes without a moving football.
Work on one height at a time.
successIndicators: Keep both thumbs behind the football.
Apply the technique at chest and overhead height.
matchApplication: Strong thumb positioning forms the base of secure chest and overhead marking. Poor thumb alignment creates a central gap that allows the football to pass through the hands under speed or pressure.

title: Low-to-High Marking Reaction
primarySkill: Reacting quickly to unexpected changes in marking height
objective: Develop rapid recognition and adjustment when the football arrives at a different height from the player’s initial expectation.
groundSize: Pairs operate six to eight metres apart within marked lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate reactive delivery and technique correction
setup:
Organise players into pairs.
Position partners six to eight metres apart.
The feeder may deliver the football low, chest height or overhead.
The feeder does not announce the height.
Deliveries should remain safe and controllable.
The marker begins in a neutral ready position.
Change roles after twelve feeds.
howTheDrillWorks:
The marker watches the feeder’s preparation.
The feeder delivers the football at one of three heights.
The marker identifies the flight immediately.
The feet and body adjust to the football’s line.
The player selects the appropriate hand position.
A low, chest or overhead mark is attempted.
The football is cushioned and secured.
The marker returns it to the feeder.
Complete four approximate deliveries at each height in random order.
Change roles and repeat.
coachingPoints: Begin from a neutral athletic stance.
Read the football rather than guessing the delivery.
Keep the hands adaptable until the height is clear.
Lower through the knees for low footballs.
Extend in front for chest marks.
Reach above eye level for overhead marks.
Move the feet to support the chosen technique.
Secure possession before resetting.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the marker watches the feeder.
Whether the player recognises the height early.
Whether hand position adjusts correctly.
Whether the feet and body support the mark.
Whether the player reacts late after guessing incorrectly.
Whether the football is cushioned.
Whether technique remains stable across all heights.
progressions: Add a forward or backward adjustment.
Include one bounce or imperfect flight.
regressions: Keep every delivery directly in front.
matchApplication: Football flight can change due to pressure, wind, poor contact or deflection. Players must react to the actual delivery rather than committing too early to one marking method.

title: Moving Low Mark
primarySkill: Completing a low mark while moving towards the football
objective: Develop the ability to maintain forward movement, lower the body and secure a football arriving below waist height.
groundSize: Lanes approximately 15 metres long and six metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate moving-low-mark instruction
setup:
Organise players into groups of three to five.
Position the feeder at one end of the lane.
The marker begins eight to ten metres away.
Mark a low receiving zone three metres in front of the marker.
The feeder delivers a controlled low kick or skidding hand feed into the receiving zone.
A third player assists with rotation.
The marker must continue moving through the mark.
Ensure the surface is safe for low body movement.
howTheDrillWorks:
The marker begins a controlled lead towards the feeder.
The feeder delivers the football below waist height.
The marker tracks the football while moving.
The player shortens the final steps.
The knees and hips flex to lower the body.
Both hands move below and in front of the football.
The mark is completed while forward movement continues.
The football is secured before the player rises.
If the football spills, the player immediately continues into a ground-ball collection.
Rotate roles after each repetition.
coachingPoints: Track the football from release.
Shorten the final steps to maintain balance.
Lower through the knees and hips.
Move the hands in front of the legs.
Point the fingers down or slightly forwards.
Keep the body behind the football.
Secure possession before rising.
Continue into a ground-ball recovery if the mark is missed.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the marker times the movement.
Whether the final steps become shorter.
Whether the player lowers correctly.
Whether hands meet the football in front.
Whether the body remains behind the line.
Whether possession is secured before rising.
Whether missed marks are recovered immediately.
progressions: Require a play-on handball after securing the mark.
Score both clean marks and immediate recoveries.
regressions: Keep the delivery directly in front.
Allow the marker to begin in a lowered stance.
successIndicators: Lower through the knees and hips.
matchApplication: Low kicks to leading players require controlled deceleration and clean hands. Correct technique allows the receiver to maintain momentum and remain competitive if the football reaches ground level.

title: Mark and Return Accuracy
primarySkill: Completing a mark and returning the football accurately to a teammate
objective: Develop the complete sequence of marking securely, regaining balance and returning an accurate disposal without rushing the post-mark action.
groundSize: Pairs operate eight to fifteen metres apart within marked lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate marking and disposal-sequence observation
setup:
Organise players into pairs.
Position partners eight metres apart for younger players and up to fifteen metres apart for experienced groups.
Mark a target gate around each player.
One player kicks to the partner.
The receiver completes the mark, secures possession and returns the football accurately.
The football should remain inside the partner’s marking gate.
Players continue alternating without fixed feeder and receiver roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A delivers a controlled kick to Player B.
Player B tracks and marks the football.
The player secures possession with two hands.
Player B regains balance and moves behind the mark if required.
The next kick is prepared without unnecessary delay.
Player B returns the football through Player A’s target gate.
Player A marks and repeats the process.
Players count consecutive completed mark-and-return sequences.
Reset the count after a dropped mark or missed target gate.
Complete two or three timed rounds.
coachingPoints: Complete the mark before preparing the return.
Secure possession with two hands.
Regain a balanced kicking position.
Keep the head up to locate the teammate.
Use an appropriate kick for the distance.
Deliver into the partner’s marking zone.
Communicate before each return.
Do not rush the kick because the mark was clean.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the mark is completed cleanly.
Whether the player remains balanced after the mark.
Whether the football is organised efficiently.
Whether the return kick is accurate.
Whether the teammate can mark without excessive adjustment.
Whether communication remains consistent.
Whether players rush as the consecutive count increases.
progressions: Add one movement step before the mark.
Compete for the longest clean sequence.
regressions: Use a handball return for younger players.
matchApplication: Marking is normally followed by another decision and disposal. Players must secure possession before delivering accurately to maintain team control.

title: Forty-Five-Degree Lead Mark
primarySkill: Timing and completing an angled lead mark
objective: Develop the ability to lead at a 45-degree angle, create a clear kicking lane and complete a mark while moving across and towards the ball carrier.
groundSize: Stations approximately 18 metres long and 12 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate lead-angle and delivery coaching
setup:
Position the kicker at one end of the station.
Place a marker at a starting cone approximately twelve metres away and slightly wider.
Mark two 45-degree lead gates, one to the left and one to the right.
A third player waits behind the kicker or acts as a return player.
The coach or kicker nominates the lead side.
The marker leads diagonally towards the selected gate.
Rotate roles after each repetition.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker secures possession and looks towards the marker.
The marker establishes eye contact.
The lead begins towards the nominated 45-degree gate.
The marker accelerates and presents both hands.
The kicker delivers the football into the angled running path.
The marker turns the chest and hands towards the football.
The mark is completed while moving through the gate.
The football is secured before deceleration.
The marker carries the football to the kicking line.
Repeat to both lead sides.
coachingPoints: Begin the lead only when the kicker is ready.
Attack the space at a genuine angle.
Accelerate strongly from the starting cone.
Present the hands and communicate.
The kicker should lead the player into the gate.
Turn the upper body enough to face the football without losing the running line.
Complete the mark before turning away.
Practise both left- and right-side leads.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the marker establishes visual connection.
Whether the lead angle creates a clear lane.
Whether acceleration produces separation.
Whether the kicker delivers into the running path.
Whether the marker aligns the hands and chest.
Whether possession is secured while moving.
Whether both lead sides are practised.
progressions: Allow the marker to choose the lead side.
Add a double lead before the 45-degree movement.
regressions: Complete the movement at jogging pace.
successIndicators: Time the lead from the kicker’s readiness.
matchApplication: Angled leads create separation and open a safer kicking lane than running directly at the ball carrier. They are commonly used by forwards, midfielders and defenders presenting from congestion.

title: Marking Triangle Rotation
primarySkill: Marking and repositioning within a three-player possession triangle
objective: Develop repeated marking, disposal and repositioning within a simple three-player structure that requires players to prepare before the football arrives.
groundSize: Triangles with sides approximately eight to fifteen metres long.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate flow and rotation management
setup:
Organise players into groups of three.
Mark a triangle using three cones.
Place one player at each cone.
One player begins with the football.
The player receiving the mark should move one or two steps towards the football.
After kicking, the disposer moves towards the next cone or follows the nominated rotation.
Begin with one direction before reversing.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A kicks to Player B.
Player B moves towards the football and completes the mark.
Player A follows the disposal towards Player B’s cone.
Player B secures possession and turns towards Player C.
Player B kicks accurately to Player C.
Player C moves and marks.
Player B follows towards Player C’s cone.
The pattern continues around the triangle.
Reverse the direction after two minutes.
Count consecutive clean marks and accurate kicks.
coachingPoints: Prepare the hands before the football arrives.
Move towards the football rather than waiting flat-footed.
Secure the mark before turning to the next target.
Turn the feet and body towards the next teammate.
Deliver accurately into the marking area.
Follow the disposal promptly.
Communicate before every kick.
Maintain safe spacing between groups.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players prepare before receiving.
Whether receivers move towards the football.
Whether marks are secured before turning.
Whether disposal accuracy supports the next mark.
Whether players follow the rotation correctly.
Whether communication remains consistent.
Whether the triangle maintains continuous flow.
progressions: Allow receivers to lead away from their cone.
matchApplication: Players must often mark, reorient and connect with the next teammate while repositioning into support. The triangle introduces simple possession flow and movement after disposal.

title: Four-Corner Marking Chain
primarySkill: Maintaining marking accuracy and movement through a four-player possession chain
objective: Develop a continuous marking chain in which players lead, secure possession, identify the next target and rotate through four field positions.
groundSize: Squares approximately twelve to twenty metres on each side.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced flow, lead timing and rotation management
setup:
Organise players into groups of four or more.
Mark a square with one player at each corner.
Place a lead marker two to three metres inside each corner.
Player A begins with the football.
The next receiver leads from the corner towards the internal marker.
After kicking, the disposer follows towards the receiver’s starting corner.
Continue clockwise before reversing.
Add additional players behind corner cones if group numbers require.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player B leads from the corner towards the internal marker.
Player A kicks into Player B’s lead.
Player B marks while moving.
Player A follows the kick towards Player B’s original corner.
Player C begins the next lead.
Player B turns, balances and delivers to Player C.
The sequence continues around all four corners.
Players communicate before every lead and delivery.
Reverse the direction after several completed rotations.
Count complete circuits without a dropped mark or missed target.
coachingPoints: The next lead should begin as the ball carrier secures possession.
Lead towards the internal marker rather than remaining on the corner.
Deliver the football into the receiver’s path.
Secure the mark before turning.
Reorient the feet towards the next target.
Follow every kick to maintain rotation.
Maintain awareness of the adjacent groups and footballs.
Use both clockwise and anticlockwise directions.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the next receiver leads at the correct time.
Whether the football is delivered into the lead.
Whether marks are completed while moving.
Whether ball carriers balance before the next kick.
Whether players follow the correct rotation.
Whether both directions are performed effectively.
Whether the chain remains continuous.
progressions: Introduce chest, overhead and low marking calls.
regressions: Predetermine lead timing with a coach call.
Complete the activity in one direction only.
successIndicators: Maintain the chain in both directions.
matchApplication: Continuous possession requires players to prepare leads before the ball carrier is ready to dispose. Accurate kicking and secure marking allow the team to move the football without unnecessary delay.

title: Marking Fundamentals Integration Assessment
primarySkill: Assessing integrated fundamental marking technique, movement and possession continuity
objective: Assess whether players can combine clean hand technique, body positioning, movement, varied marking heights and accurate post-mark disposal within fundamental marking activities.
groundSize: Five assessment stations arranged within an area approximately 40 metres × 30 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced technical assessment and feedback management
setup:
Establish five assessment stations:
Station 1: One-grab chest and overhead marking.
Station 2: Reactive low, chest and overhead marks.
Station 3: Moving low and straight-lead marks.
Station 4: Forty-five-degree lead marking.
Station 5: Mark-and-return possession chain.
Divide players evenly between stations.
Assign a coach or trained observer where possible.
Standardise delivery distances and target areas.
Allow one practice repetition before formal scoring.
Record technical completion and movement quality separately.
Adjust football size and delivery speed to the age group.
howTheDrillWorks:
At Station 1, each player completes four chest and four overhead one-grab marks.
At Station 2, each player completes six unpredictable-height marking attempts.
At Station 3, each player completes three moving low marks and three straight-lead marks.
At Station 4, each player completes two leads to the left and two to the right.
At Station 5, each player participates in a timed mark-and-return possession chain.
Observers assess tracking, footwork, hand shape, first-contact control, cushioning and security.
Post-mark balance and return accuracy are also recorded.
Players rotate only after all group members complete the station.
Each player receives one identified strength and one priority correction.
Players repeat the station linked to their lowest score.
coachingPoints: Apply consistent standards across every station.
Assess the player’s preparation before the football arrives.
Record whether the feet position the body correctly.
Judge hand position according to football height.
Distinguish one-grab control from eventual possession.
Assess whether moving players continue through the mark.
Include post-mark security and balance.
Separate poor delivery from player error.
Feedback should identify one specific technical action.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players track the football continuously.
Whether hand shape changes appropriately.
Whether the football is contacted in front or at the highest comfortable point.
Whether marks are secured without juggling.
Whether moving players maintain balance.
Whether leads are timed correctly.
Whether post-mark disposal is accurate.
Whether feedback is applied during the repeated station.
progressions: Repeat the assessment later in the training phase.
Use video review for hand shape and body position.
regressions: Separate low, chest and overhead testing.
successIndicators: Secure low, chest and overhead footballs.
matchApplication: Fundamental marking requires more than catching a stationary football. Players must recognise height, move into line, secure first contact, lead effectively and maintain possession through the next action.

title: Moving Chest Mark
primarySkill: Completing a chest mark while moving at controlled speed
objective: Develop the ability to maintain movement, present the hands early and secure a chest-height football without stopping before contact.
groundSize: Lanes approximately 18 metres long and six metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate movement and delivery timing
setup:
Organise players into groups of three to five.
Position the kicker at one end of the lane.
The marker begins ten to twelve metres away.
Mark a three-metre receiving zone between the kicker and marker.
A third player waits behind the kicker or at the far end for rotation.
The marker runs through the receiving zone.
The kicker aims to deliver the football between waist and chest height.
Players rotate after every repetition.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker establishes possession and signals readiness.
The marker begins moving towards the receiving zone.
The player accelerates into the lead and calls for the football.
The kicker delivers the football into the marker’s running path.
The marker tracks the football while continuing forward.
Both hands extend in front of the body.
The player cushions and secures the football at chest height.
The marker continues through the receiving zone before decelerating.
The football is carried to the kicking line.
Players rotate and repeat.
coachingPoints: Begin the lead only when the kicker is balanced.
Accelerate during the first few steps.
Present both hands early.
Keep the eyes on the football while running.
Meet the football in front of the body.
Cushion through the elbows.
Continue moving through the mark.
Secure possession before decelerating or turning.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the lead is timed from the kicker’s readiness.
Whether the marker accelerates.
Whether the kick enters the running path.
Whether both hands are presented.
Whether the marker continues moving through contact.
Whether the football is cushioned and secured.
Whether deceleration remains balanced.
progressions: Require a quick play-on after the mark.
Deliver slightly left or right of the running line.
regressions: Slow the movement to a jog.
Allow the marker to begin closer.
matchApplication: Players frequently mark while leading towards the ball carrier. Maintaining movement through the mark helps create separation and allows the next possession to begin more quickly.

title: Lateral Lead Mark
primarySkill: Completing a mark while leading laterally across the ball carrier
objective: Develop the ability to create width through a lateral lead, turn the body towards the football and secure the mark without losing the running line.
groundSize: Stations approximately 18 metres long and 14 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate lead-angle and body-orientation coaching
setup:
Position the kicker at one end of the station.
The marker begins twelve metres away and five metres to one side.
Mark a lateral lead gate across the kicker’s field of vision.
A third player waits as a return player.
The marker leads across the ground rather than directly at the kicker.
The kicker aims to deliver the football into the lateral path.
Mirror the setup for both left-to-right and right-to-left movement.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker gains possession and looks towards the marker.
The marker begins a lateral lead across the station.
The player accelerates and communicates.
The kicker delivers the football towards the lead gate.
The marker rotates the chest and shoulders towards the football while maintaining the running line.
Both hands extend towards the kick.
The mark is completed in front of the body.
The player continues through the gate.
The football is returned and roles rotate.
Repeat in both lateral directions.
coachingPoints: Begin the lead after visual connection with the kicker.
Accelerate across the ground rather than drifting.
Maintain separation from the kicker’s direct line.
Turn the chest enough to face the football.
Avoid rotating the entire body so far that running speed is lost.
Present both hands early.
Meet the football in front.
Continue through the lead gate after marking.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the marker times the lateral lead.
Whether genuine acceleration occurs.
Whether the player maintains the lead line.
Whether the chest and hands face the football.
Whether the kick is placed ahead of the marker.
Whether the mark is completed in motion.
Whether both movement directions are practised.
progressions: Allow the marker to choose the lead direction.
Require the marker to play on after the mark.
regressions: Complete the movement at jogging pace.
successIndicators: Receive the football ahead of the body.
matchApplication: Lateral leads create space across half-forward, the wings and defensive exits. Players must maintain speed while turning the upper body towards the football.

title: Double-Lead Marking
primarySkill: Using a change of direction to create separation before marking
objective: Develop the ability to begin one lead, change direction and accelerate into a second lead before completing the mark.
groundSize: Stations approximately 20 metres long and 15 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced lead timing and change-of-direction management
setup:
Position the kicker at one end of the station.
The marker begins twelve to fifteen metres away.
Mark one initial lead gate and one secondary gate in the opposite direction.
The marker begins towards the first gate before changing direction.
The kicker holds the football until the second lead is established.
A third player assists with rotation.
Practise changes of direction to both sides.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker establishes possession.
The marker begins the initial lead towards the first gate.
The player plants, lowers the centre of gravity and changes direction.
The marker accelerates towards the secondary gate.
The kicker delivers into the second lead.
The marker communicates and presents both hands.
The football is marked while moving through the secondary gate.
The player secures possession before decelerating.
Roles rotate after each repetition.
Repeat with the lead pattern reversed.
coachingPoints: Sell the initial lead with genuine speed.
Lower the hips before changing direction.
Plant with control rather than slipping or overstriding.
Reaccelerate strongly out of the change.
The kicker should wait for separation before delivering.
Present the hands during the second lead.
Keep the eyes on the football after the kick.
Continue through the final gate.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the first lead appears genuine.
Whether the marker decelerates safely.
Whether the change of direction is balanced.
Whether reacceleration creates separation.
Whether the kicker waits for the second lead.
Whether the mark is completed in motion.
Whether both change directions are used.
progressions: Allow the marker to choose the second lead.
Add a third possible lead gate.
Require a quick play-on after the mark.
Introduce a live kick decision between two markers.
regressions: Increase the space around the turn.
successIndicators: Complete the mark in the second lead.
matchApplication: Double leads help forwards and midfielders lose close-checking opponents. The second movement must be timed with the ball carrier and performed at greater speed than the first.

title: Mark-and-Go Corridor
primarySkill: Marking while moving and immediately continuing through a corridor
objective: Develop the ability to complete a moving mark, secure possession and continue forward without losing control or balance.
groundSize: Corridors approximately 25 metres long and eight metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced marking-to-play-on sequence management
setup:
Mark a 25-metre corridor with a receiving gate in the first half and a disposal gate at the far end.
Player A begins with the football.
Player B starts ten metres ahead.
Player C waits beyond the disposal gate.
Player D acts as a return or rotation player.
Player B leads through the receiving gate.
After marking, Player B continues forward and delivers to Player C.
Players follow the football through the positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player B begins a forward lead.
Player A kicks into the receiving gate.
Player B marks while maintaining forward movement.
The player secures the football with two hands.
Player B continues through the corridor.
The football is organised while running.
Player B delivers to Player C through the disposal gate.
Player C marks and carries the football to the starting line.
All players rotate forward one position.
Continue in a flowing sequence.
coachingPoints: Time the lead from the ball carrier’s readiness.
Meet the football in front.
Secure possession before increasing speed.
Continue forward without taking uncontrolled steps.
Keep the football close to the body while running.
Lift the eyes to find the next target.
Balance before the next disposal.
Do not rush the second action at the expense of the mark.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the lead is timed correctly.
Whether the mark is completed in movement.
Whether possession is secured before acceleration.
Whether the player keeps the football protected.
Whether the next target is identified.
Whether the final disposal is balanced and accurate.
Whether the rotation remains continuous.
progressions: Narrow the receiving and disposal gates.
Allow the receiver to choose between two final targets.
regressions: Use a hand feed for the first mark.
Allow the marker to slow more after receiving.
matchApplication: Players often mark during transition and need to continue immediately. A controlled mark-and-go action can preserve team speed before the opposition resets.

title: Crossing Leads Marking
primarySkill: Maintaining clear marking lanes when two players cross leads
objective: Develop coordinated crossing leads in which two markers create options without colliding, crowding the ball carrier’s vision or entering the same receiving lane.
groundSize: Stations approximately 22 metres long and 18 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced lead coordination and kicker-choice management
setup:
Position the kicker at one end.
Place two markers at separate starting cones, one left and one right.
Mark two crossing lead gates at different depths.
One marker leads shallow across the ground.
The second marker leads deeper in the opposite direction.
A fourth player acts as the return player.
The kicker chooses the clearest option.
Rotate all roles regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker gains possession and scans both markers.
The shallow marker begins the first crossing lead.
The deeper marker begins shortly afterwards through the second lane.
Both players communicate and maintain separate depths.
The kicker selects the clearest leading option.
The football is delivered into that player’s path.
The selected marker completes the mark.
The unused marker clears the lane and becomes the next support player.
Players reset and rotate roles.
Repeat with the lead depths reversed.
coachingPoints: Crossing leads must operate at different depths.
The first lead should not block the second.
Both markers should communicate clearly.
The kicker should scan both options before choosing.
Avoid predetermined disposal when one option is covered or poorly timed.
Lead at genuine speed.
The unused marker should continue clearing space.
Deliver into the selected marker’s forward path.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the leads begin in a coordinated sequence.
Whether players maintain different depths.
Whether running lanes remain separated.
Whether the kicker scans both options.
Whether the correct option is selected.
Whether the kick leads the receiver.
Whether the unused marker clears space.
progressions: Allow markers to choose their own lead sequence.
Require the kicker to hold the football until one lane opens.
Continue play after the selected mark.
successIndicators: Allow the kicker to select clearly.
matchApplication: Crossing leads can move defenders and create space, but only when the leading players maintain separate lanes and the ball carrier reads the developing options.

title: Backward-Flight Marking
primarySkill: Tracking and marking a football while moving backwards
objective: Develop the ability to track a football travelling over the player’s initial position, move backwards safely and complete the mark without losing balance.
groundSize: Lanes approximately 18 metres long and eight metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced flight, footwork and safety management
setup:
Position the feeder eight to ten metres in front of the marker.
The marker begins at a central starting cone.
Mark a rear receiving zone three to five metres behind the marker.
A third player acts as a safety observer or rotation player.
The feeder delivers a controlled lob or kick over the marker’s starting position.
The marker must turn or backpedal safely into the receiving zone.
Maintain large separation between lanes.
howTheDrillWorks:
The marker begins facing the feeder.
The feeder delivers the football over the marker’s initial position.
The marker identifies the deeper flight.
The player uses short backward steps or a controlled turn to move towards the drop point.
The marker keeps the eyes on the football.
The hands rise early.
The football is marked overhead or at chest height in the rear zone.
The player secures possession and regains balance.
The football is returned and roles rotate.
Repeat with slight left and right variation.
coachingPoints: Read the deeper flight immediately.
Use short backward steps only over limited distance.
Turn and run when the football travels further behind.
Maintain awareness of the space behind.
Keep the head stable and eyes on the football.
Raise the hands before the football descends.
Avoid leaning backwards excessively.
Secure possession before stopping or changing direction.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the player recognises the deeper flight.
Whether backward footwork remains safe.
Whether the player turns when required.
Whether the eyes remain on the football.
Whether the body reaches the drop point.
Whether the mark is completed from balance.
Whether the lanes remain clear.
progressions: Use controlled kicks instead of lobbed feeds.
Require an immediate turn after the mark.
Begin from a moving starting position.
regressions: Allow the marker to turn immediately rather than backpedal.
Practise without a football to establish safe footwork.
successIndicators: Select backpedal or turn-and-run footwork appropriately.
matchApplication: Defenders and midfielders often need to track kicks travelling over their initial position. Safe footwork and early flight judgement are essential when marking while moving towards defensive goal.

title: Turn-and-Track Mark
primarySkill: Turning from an initial forward-facing position to track and mark a football behind
objective: Develop the ability to turn efficiently, locate the football and complete a mark after beginning with the body facing away from the expected drop zone.
groundSize: Lanes approximately 20 metres long and eight metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced turning, flight-location and safety coaching
setup:
Position the marker facing a coach or cue player.
The kicker stands behind the marker and slightly to one side.
Mark a receiving zone eight to twelve metres behind the marker.
The coach gives a left or right turn cue.
The kicker delivers the football into the rear zone after the cue.
A third player assists with rotation and safety.
Alternate turn directions regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The marker begins facing the coach.
The coach provides a left or right turn cue.
The player turns over the nominated shoulder.
The marker immediately locates the football.
The player accelerates towards the receiving zone.
Running speed is adjusted according to the flight.
The hands rise as the football descends.
The mark is completed and secured.
The player returns the football and roles rotate.
Repeat with both turn directions and varied flight.
coachingPoints: Turn with the feet and hips rather than twisting only through the upper body.
Locate the football immediately after turning.
Accelerate once the flight is identified.
Avoid turning through the same side every time.
Adjust speed as the drop point becomes clear.
Maintain awareness of other players and lanes.
Raise the hands early.
Arrive beneath the football in balance.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the player turns in the nominated direction.
Whether the football is located quickly.
Whether acceleration follows the turn.
Whether running speed is adjusted.
Whether the player reaches the correct drop point.
Whether the mark is completed cleanly.
Whether both shoulders are used comfortably.
progressions: Remove the verbal direction and use visual cues.
Add a passive opponent beginning beside the marker.
regressions: Allow the marker to watch the initial release.
Practise the turn without a moving football.
matchApplication: Players frequently begin facing their opponent, the ball carrier or the wrong direction before a high kick is released. Efficient turning and rapid football location allow them to recover into the marking contest.

title: Repeat-Lead Marking Chain
primarySkill: Completing repeated leads and marks within a continuous possession chain
objective: Develop the ability to recover after a disposal, create another lead and complete repeated moving marks without losing technical quality.
groundSize: A rectangular area approximately 30 metres long and 18 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced workload, rotation and timing management
setup:
Mark two parallel possession lanes.
Place three players in each lane: kicker, middle receiver and end receiver.
Mark a lead gate in front of each receiving position.
The middle player must mark, dispose and then create a second lead in the opposite direction.
Use one football in each lane.
Players rotate after a complete end-to-end sequence.
Maintain sufficient distance between the two lanes.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A kicks to Player B’s forward lead.
Player B marks while moving through the first gate.
Player B turns, balances and kicks to Player C.
Player C marks at the far end.
Player B immediately changes direction and leads back towards Player C.
Player C kicks into Player B’s return lead.
Player B marks again while moving.
Player B returns the football to Player A.
Players rotate positions.
Continue for repeated timed rounds.
coachingPoints: Time each lead from the ball carrier’s possession.
Accelerate into both the first and return leads.
Secure every mark before turning.
Recover quickly after disposal.
Maintain football tracking under fatigue.
Kicks should lead the receiver rather than force them to stop.
Use controlled deceleration before changing direction.
Preserve marking quality across repeated efforts.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether both leads are timed correctly.
Whether Player B accelerates in both directions.
Whether marks are completed cleanly.
Whether the player recovers promptly after disposal.
Whether the return kick is placed correctly.
Whether technique deteriorates across repetitions.
Whether rotations remain organised.
progressions: Add a third lead within the sequence.
matchApplication: Players often need to lead, dispose and work again during the same possession chain. Repeat movement increases the chance of becoming involved in multiple phases.

title: Moving Mark Through Choice Gates
primarySkill: Selecting and completing a moving mark through one of multiple lead gates
objective: Develop the ability of the marker and kicker to read space, select an available movement lane and connect through an appropriate lead.
groundSize: Stations approximately 22 metres long and 18 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced scanning, lane selection and delivery management
setup:
Position the kicker at one end of the station.
Place the marker at a central starting cone.
Mark three lead gates:
Straight.
Left angle.
Right angle.
Position one shadow lane-closer near the gates.
The lane-closer blocks one gate by standing inside it before the lead begins.
The marker and kicker must identify the remaining options.
Rotate all roles after several repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker gains possession and scans the lead gates.
The lane-closer occupies one gate.
The marker scans the available space.
The marker selects an open gate and begins the lead.
The kicker confirms the movement and delivers into the selected lane.
The marker tracks the football and adjusts the body.
The mark is completed while moving through the gate.
The lane-closer remains stationary during the introductory version.
Players reset and change roles.
Repeat with different gates removed.
coachingPoints: Scan the available space before leading.
Do not lead directly into the occupied gate.
Communicate the selected lane.
The kicker must read the same option.
Begin the lead with acceleration.
Deliver into the running path.
Adjust marking technique to the football’s height.
Continue through the gate after securing possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the marker identifies the closed gate.
Whether the selected lead creates clear space.
Whether the kicker recognises the movement.
Whether communication occurs.
Whether the football is placed into the lead.
Whether the mark is completed in motion.
Whether players use all available gate types.
progressions: Allow the lane-closer to move after the lead begins.
Remove the coloured gates and use open space only.
matchApplication: Players must lead according to available space rather than repeating predetermined movement. The ball carrier and receiver need shared recognition of the open lane.

title: Moving Marking Competency Assessment
primarySkill: Assessing marking execution while leading, changing direction and tracking varied football flight
objective: Assess each player’s ability to time movement, reach the football’s line, complete a secure mark and continue the possession across varied moving-mark situations.
groundSize: Five assessment stations arranged within an area approximately 50 metres × 35 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert movement assessment and feedback management
setup:
Establish five assessment stations:
Station 1: Moving chest mark.
Station 2: Lateral and 45-degree lead marking.
Station 3: Double-lead marking.
Station 4: Backward-flight and turn-and-track marking.
Station 5: Mark-and-go possession corridor.
Divide players evenly between stations.
Assign a coach or trained observer where possible.
Standardise movement distances and delivery difficulty.
Allow one practice repetition at each station.
Record movement quality and marking execution separately.
Repeat unsuitable deliveries rather than scoring them as player errors.
howTheDrillWorks:
At Station 1, each player completes four moving chest marks.
At Station 2, each player completes two lateral and two angled leads on each side.
At Station 3, each player completes four double-lead repetitions.
At Station 4, each player completes two backward-flight and two turn-and-track marks from each turning side.
At Station 5, each player completes four mark-and-go corridor repetitions.
Observers score lead timing, acceleration, footwork, flight judgement, hand position and security.
Post-mark balance and continuation are also recorded.
Players rotate after all members complete the required attempts.
Each player receives one movement strength and one priority correction.
Players repeat the station linked to their lowest score.
coachingPoints: Assess movement before the football is delivered.
Record whether the lead begins from the kicker’s readiness.
Evaluate acceleration and change-of-direction quality.
Observe whether the player reaches the football’s line.
Judge whether the correct marking technique is selected.
Include first-contact control and post-mark security.
Assess whether players continue through moving marks.
Distinguish poor delivery from poor movement.
Provide feedback linked to a specific observable behaviour.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players establish visual connection with the kicker.
Whether leads are timed correctly.
Whether movement creates separation.
Whether players change direction safely.
Whether backward and turning footwork remains controlled.
Whether the football is tracked continuously.
Whether marks are completed cleanly.
Whether players remain balanced after possession.
Whether feedback is applied during reassessment.
progressions: Include live choice between multiple lead options.
Repeat the assessment later in the training phase.
successIndicators: Time leads from the ball carrier’s readiness.
Secure possession before the next action.
