matchApplication: Moving marking combines technical hands with lead timing, acceleration, flight judgement and body control. This assessment determines whether players can apply fundamental marking technique while movement patterns become more demanding.

title: Curved Lead Mark
primarySkill: Using a curved lead to create separation and complete a moving mark
objective: Develop the ability to use a curved running pattern to move away from a defender’s direct line and present a clear marking option to the ball carrier.
groundSize: Stations approximately 22 metres long and 16 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced running-line and delivery management
setup:
Position the kicker at one end of the station.
Place the marker approximately fourteen metres away.
Mark a curved lead path using three cones.
The path begins laterally before curving towards the ball carrier.
Place a receiving gate at the end of the curved path.
A third player assists with football return and rotation.
Mirror the setup so players practise curves from both sides.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker secures possession and scans the marker.
The marker establishes visual connection.
The marker begins laterally along the first section of the curved path.
The player accelerates and curves towards the receiving gate.
The kicker delivers the football into the final section of the lead.
The marker turns the chest and hands towards the kick.
The mark is completed while moving through the gate.
The player secures possession before decelerating.
Roles rotate after each repetition.
Repeat from both curved-lead directions.
coachingPoints: Begin the lead when the kicker is balanced and able to deliver.
Use the initial lateral movement to create a different angle.
Accelerate through the curve rather than slowing around it.
Keep the curved path smooth rather than making several sharp turns.
Re-establish direct vision of the football during the final section.
Present both hands early.
The kicker should deliver into the final running line.
Continue through the receiving gate after marking.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the marker times the lead correctly.
Whether the curved pattern creates a clear kicking lane.
Whether speed is maintained through the curve.
Whether the marker turns the body towards the football.
Whether the kick enters the final running path.
Whether the mark is completed in motion.
Whether both curved directions are practised.
progressions: Allow the marker to select the curve direction.
Increase lead speed and kicking distance.
successIndicators: Maintain speed through the change of angle.
Perform the skill in both directions.
matchApplication: Curved leads allow forwards and midfielders to move away from direct defensive pressure while still presenting towards the ball carrier. The changing angle can create separation and open a safer delivery lane.

title: Stop-Start Lead Mark
primarySkill: Using a controlled stop and reacceleration to create marking separation
objective: Develop the ability to alter running speed, pause under control and accelerate again into a marking lead.
groundSize: Stations approximately 20 metres long and twelve metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced pace-change and delivery timing
setup:
Position the kicker at one end of the station.
The marker begins twelve to fourteen metres away.
Mark an initial lead cone, a stop zone and a final receiving gate.
The marker leads towards the first cone, controls the movement briefly in the stop zone and then accelerates through the final gate.
The kicker must wait until the player reaccelerates.
A third player assists with rotation.
Practise final leads to both sides.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker gains possession and looks towards the marker.
The marker begins an initial lead towards the stop zone.
The player shortens the steps and controls momentum.
The marker pauses briefly without becoming upright or inactive.
The player then accelerates sharply towards the final receiving gate.
The kicker delivers into the renewed lead.
The marker presents both hands and tracks the football.
The mark is completed while moving through the gate.
Roles rotate after each repetition.
Repeat with varied stop-zone and final-gate directions.
coachingPoints: The initial lead must be genuine enough to influence a defender.
Shorten the steps before stopping.
Keep the knees flexed and the body ready to move again.
Avoid standing fully upright during the pause.
Reaccelerate strongly through the first three steps.
The kicker should deliver only after renewed separation appears.
Present both hands early during the final movement.
Continue through the mark.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the initial lead is performed at genuine speed.
Whether deceleration remains balanced.
Whether the player stays physically ready during the pause.
Whether reacceleration is immediate and powerful.
Whether the kicker waits for the second movement.
Whether the mark is completed while moving.
Whether both final directions are used.
progressions: Vary the length of the pause.
Allow the marker to choose the final direction.
matchApplication: Changes of pace can create separation without a major change of direction. A defender who relaxes during the pause may be unable to respond to the second acceleration.

title: Recovering Forward Mark
primarySkill: Recovering from backward movement to attack and mark the football forward
objective: Develop the ability to move backwards initially, recognise a shorter football and recover forward quickly enough to complete the mark.
groundSize: Lanes approximately 20 metres long and eight metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced recovery movement and flight-reading management
setup:
Position the feeder at one end of the lane.
The marker begins ten metres away.
Mark a rear movement cone three metres behind the marker.
Mark a forward receiving gate three to five metres in front.
The marker begins moving towards the rear cone.
The feeder then delivers a shorter football towards the forward gate.
A third player assists with rotation and lane safety.
Use only controlled deliveries.
howTheDrillWorks:
The marker begins facing the feeder.
On the coach’s signal, the marker moves backwards towards the rear cone.
The feeder delivers the football short towards the forward gate.
The marker recognises the change in flight.
The player plants, turns the hips and accelerates forward.
The marker tracks the football while attacking the receiving point.
Both hands extend towards the football.
The mark is completed while moving forward.
The player secures possession and roles rotate.
Repeat with slight left and right variation.
coachingPoints: Maintain a balanced body position during the initial backward movement.
Read the football immediately after release.
Use a short plant step before changing direction.
Turn through the hips and feet.
Accelerate directly towards the drop point.
Keep the head stable during the change.
Meet the football in front.
Continue forward through the mark.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether backward movement remains balanced.
Whether the shorter flight is recognised early.
Whether the player changes direction efficiently.
Whether acceleration is direct.
Whether the marker reaches the football’s line.
Whether the mark is completed in front.
Whether the lane remains safe.

regressions: Keep the receiving gate directly in front.
matchApplication: Players tracking deeper space may need to recover forward when a kick drops short. Early recognition and decisive forward movement can turn a difficult possession into a clean intercept or leading mark.

title: Moving Mark and Immediate Handball
primarySkill: Completing a moving mark and immediately releasing a teammate by handball
objective: Develop the ability to secure a moving mark, recognise nearby support and complete a legal handball without compromising control of the mark.
groundSize: Corridors approximately 22 metres long and twelve metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced mark-to-disposal sequence management
setup:
Player A begins with the football.
Player B starts ten metres ahead and leads towards a receiving gate.
Player C begins behind and outside Player B as a handball support runner.
Player D waits beyond the finishing gate.
Player A kicks to Player B’s lead.
Player C runs past after the mark is secured.
Players rotate through all positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player B begins the lead.
Player A delivers into the receiving gate.
Player B completes the moving mark.
The player secures possession with two hands.
Player C communicates and accelerates past on the outside.
Player B identifies the support runner.
The football is organised onto the correct supporting hand.
Player B handballs into Player C’s forward path.
Player C receives and connects with Player D.
Players follow the football and rotate.
coachingPoints: Complete the mark before preparing the handball.
Maintain two-hand security through initial contact.
Lift the eyes after possession is secured.
The support runner should communicate and pass outside the marker.
Use the hand that directs the football away from congestion.
Lead the support runner forward.
Keep the handball action legal and controlled.
Do not release merely because a player runs past if the option is covered.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether Player B completes the mark before organising disposal.
Whether Player C times the support run.
Whether the marker scans after possession.
Whether the appropriate hand is selected.
Whether the handball leads the runner.
Whether technique remains legal.
Whether the possession chain continues smoothly.
progressions: Add a shadow defender on the support runner.
Allow the marker to choose whether to handball or retain.
regressions: Use a hand feed for the mark.
Allow the marker to stop before handballing.
matchApplication: Players frequently mark and immediately release a teammate running past. The mark must be completed first, and the handball should create genuine forward advantage.

title: Mark, Turn and Kick to a Lead
primarySkill: Completing a mark, turning in balance and kicking to a new leading target
objective: Develop the ability to secure a mark, reorient towards the next phase and accurately connect with a teammate leading in a different direction.
groundSize: Stations approximately 25 metres long and eighteen metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced post-mark orientation and timing management
setup:
Player A begins with the football at the starting cone.
Player B starts ten metres ahead and leads towards the first gate.
Player C begins wider and beyond Player B.
Player D acts as the rotation or return player.
After Player B marks, Player C leads through either a left or right gate.
Player B must turn and deliver accurately.
Rotate all positions regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player B leads towards the first receiving gate.
Player A kicks into the lead.
Player B completes and secures the mark.
Player C begins a lead through one of the second gates.
Player B lifts the eyes and identifies the movement.
The player turns the feet and body towards Player C.
Player B balances and kicks into the second lead.
Player C completes the moving mark.
Players follow the football and rotate.
Repeat with second leads to both sides.
coachingPoints: Secure the first mark before turning.
Lift the eyes early after possession is completed.
Turn with the feet rather than twisting only through the upper body.
Establish balance before kicking.
Player C should begin the lead from Player B’s clean possession.
Deliver into the second player’s running path.
Avoid excessive delay between the mark and next kick.
Maintain accuracy while increasing the speed of the sequence.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether Player B secures the first mark.
Whether Player C times the second lead.
Whether Player B scans quickly.
Whether the turn is balanced.
Whether the kick leads Player C.
Whether the second mark is completed in motion.
Whether the chain flows without unnecessary delay.

Reduce the time available for the second kick.
Introduce kick-or-handball choice after the first mark.

Allow Player B to stop fully before turning.
matchApplication: Ball movement depends on the marking player preparing the next possession quickly. Securing, scanning and turning efficiently helps teams move the football before the opposition can reposition.

title: Three-Player Lead Replacement
primarySkill: Replacing the space vacated by a leading teammate within a three-player marking structure
objective: Develop coordinated movement in which one player leads to mark while another replaces the vacated position to maintain the possession structure.
groundSize: Triangles approximately fifteen to twenty metres on each side.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced movement and replacement management
setup:
Mark a triangle with one player at each outside cone.
Place one lead gate inside each side of the triangle.
Player A begins with the football.
Player B leads towards Player A.
As Player B leaves the starting cone, Player C moves to replace Player B’s vacated position.
After the mark, Player B identifies the replacement and delivers.
Continue the rotation around the triangle.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player B begins a lead towards Player A.
Player A kicks into Player B’s movement.
Player C moves towards Player B’s vacated outside position.
Player B completes and secures the mark.
Player B turns and scans the replacement movement.
Player C then leads from the replacement position.
Player B kicks into Player C’s lead.
Player A moves to replace Player C’s original position.
The pattern continues around the triangle.
Reverse the direction after several rotations.
coachingPoints: The next player should replace space as soon as the lead begins.
Replacement movement should not crowd the current marking lane.
The marker must secure possession before scanning the next option.
Communicate every lead and replacement.
Players should move with purpose rather than walking between cones.
Kicks must lead the next receiver.
Maintain triangle width.
Reverse direction to develop movement on both sides.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether replacement movement begins at the correct time.
Whether the vacated space is filled.
Whether players avoid crowding.
Whether the marker scans after securing possession.
Whether the next lead is timed.
Whether kicks are accurate.
Whether the structure remains balanced.
progressions: Introduce a handball option after marking.
successIndicators: Complete the pattern in both directions.
matchApplication: Effective team movement requires players to replace teammates who lead away from their position. This maintains width, preserves structure and provides the next possession option.

title: Lane-Switch Marking Chain
primarySkill: Changing lanes after a mark to continue a possession chain
objective: Develop a marking chain that shifts the football between inside and outside lanes through coordinated leads and accurate delivery.
groundSize: A rectangular area approximately thirty metres long and twenty metres wide, divided into three lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced lane, rotation and delivery management
setup:
Mark three parallel lanes: left, centre and right.
Position players at staggered starting points through each lane.
The football begins in one outside lane.
The next receiver leads diagonally into the centre lane.
A later receiver then leads towards the opposite outside lane.
Players follow their kicks into the vacated positions.
Use one football initially before adding a second group.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A begins in the left outside lane.
Player B leads diagonally from the centre lane.
Player A kicks into Player B’s lead.
Player B completes and secures the mark.
Player C leads from the right outside lane towards space ahead.
Player B turns and delivers into Player C’s movement.
Player C marks and continues the chain towards the next central player.
Players follow their disposal into the vacated position.
The football continues switching lanes along the area.
Reverse the starting side after several completed chains.
coachingPoints: Leads should change the ball’s angle rather than remain in the same lane.
Receivers should move after the previous mark is secured.
Maintain separation between adjacent players.
Secure the mark before turning.
Reorient the feet towards the next lane.
Deliver into the lead rather than at the player’s starting cone.
Follow the disposal to preserve rotation.
Maintain equal practice in both directions.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the possession changes lanes.
Whether leads begin at the correct time.
Whether players maintain spacing.
Whether markers turn in balance.
Whether kicks lead receivers.
Whether the chain remains continuous.
Whether both outside lanes are used.
progressions: Add passive defenders in selected lanes.
Allow players to choose the next lane.
matchApplication: Changing the angle of possession can move the defence and open new space. Accurate marking chains between inside and outside lanes help teams progress without becoming predictable.

title: Inside-Outside Support Marking
primarySkill: Using inside and outside leading options within a structured marking possession
objective: Develop the ability to create and select between inside and outside marking options while maintaining useful team spacing.
groundSize: Stations approximately twenty-five metres long and twenty metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced support-shape and decision management
setup:
Position the ball carrier at one end of the station.
Place one marker in an inside starting position and one in an outside starting position.
Mark an inside lead gate closer to the centre and an outside gate wider.
Add one shadow lane-closer who may discourage one option.
Place a finishing receiver beyond both lead gates.
The ball carrier chooses the safer or more advantageous marking option.
Rotate all roles regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier gains possession and scans both markers.
The inside and outside markers begin coordinated leads.
The lane-closer moves to discourage one option.
The ball carrier identifies the clearer marking lane.
The football is kicked into the selected lead.
The chosen receiver completes and secures the mark.
The unused marker repositions as the next support option.
The marking player connects with the finishing receiver.
Players follow the football and rotate.
Repeat with varied defensive positioning.
coachingPoints: Inside and outside options must remain separated.
Both markers should present genuine leads.
The ball carrier must scan before selecting.
Avoid choosing the preferred side automatically.
The outside player should maintain width.
The inside player should avoid leading into congestion.
The unused marker should remain involved.
The selected receiver must secure possession before connecting forward.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the two options remain separated.
Whether both leads are genuine.
Whether the lane-closer affects the decision.
Whether the ball carrier chooses the safer option.
Whether the football is placed into the selected lead.
Whether the unused marker repositions.
Whether possession continues effectively.

Allow the ball carrier to retain possession.
Add kick-or-handball choice after the mark.

title: Continuous End-to-End Marking Wave
primarySkill: Maintaining moving-mark execution within a continuous end-to-end possession wave

groundSize: A rectangular area approximately forty metres long and twenty metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert flow, workload and multiple-football management

Mark two end zones and three staggered receiving stations through the middle.
Divide players evenly between both ends and middle stations.
One group moves the football from End A to End B.
A second group begins in the opposite direction after a safe interval.

The next player leads from the first middle station.
The football is kicked into the lead and marked in motion.
The marking player turns and connects with the next leading station.

A new wave begins from End B in the opposite direction.
Every disposer follows the football into the next position.
Players communicate and maintain safe separation between waves.
Continue for timed work periods.
Reduce speed or football numbers if marking quality or safety deteriorates.
coachingPoints: The next lead should begin from the previous clean mark.
Deliver every kick into forward movement.
Secure possession before preparing the next disposal.
Follow every kick.
Maintain width between opposing waves.
Communicate loudly when footballs approach shared areas.
Preserve marking technique under repeated effort.
Workload should challenge players without creating unsafe congestion.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether leads begin at the correct time.
Whether kicks allow receivers to continue.
Whether marks remain clean under fatigue.
Whether players follow the rotation.
Whether opposing waves remain separated.
Whether communication prevents collisions.

title: Marking Movement and Support Assessment
primarySkill: Assessing moving-mark execution, lead variety and support connection

groundSize: Five assessment stations arranged within an area approximately sixty metres × forty metres.

Establish five assessment stations:

Divide players evenly between stations.

Standardise distances and delivery difficulty.
Allow one practice repetition before assessment.
Record movement, marking and post-mark execution separately.
Plan suitable recovery before Station 5.
howTheDrillWorks:
At Station 1, each player completes two curved leads and two stop-start leads in both directions.
At Station 2, each player completes four backward-to-forward recovery marks.
At Station 3, each player completes two mark-and-handball and two mark-and-kick actions.
At Station 4, players complete lead-replacement and lane-switch roles within a group possession chain.
At Station 5, players complete a timed continuous marking wave.
Observers assess lead timing, acceleration, body control, flight judgement, hand position and security.
Post-mark scanning, disposal and support movement are also scored.
Clearly unsuitable deliveries are repeated.
Each player receives one movement strength and one priority development action.
Players repeat the station linked to their lowest score where workload permits.
coachingPoints: Assess movement before the football is released.
Record whether each lead creates genuine separation or a clear lane.
Observe deceleration and change-of-direction safety.
Assess whether the player reaches the football’s line.
Apply full marking standards under movement.
Record whether possession is secured before the next action.
Evaluate post-mark scanning and disposal.
Include movement after disposal and positional replacement.
Assess whether technique remains stable under repeated effort.
Feedback must identify one specific observable behaviour.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players time varied leads correctly.
Whether changes of pace and direction create space.
Whether recovery footwork remains balanced.
Whether football flight is tracked continuously.
Whether moving marks are completed cleanly.
Whether the football is secured before disposal.
Whether handball and kicking connections are accurate.
Whether players replace vacated space.
Whether repeated-effort marking quality remains stable.
Whether feedback is applied during reassessment.
progressions: Add live choice between multiple support options.
Repeat the assessment later and compare results.

successIndicators: Connect accurately by hand or foot.
Maintain marking quality under repeated movement.
matchApplication: Moving marking depends on more than clean hands. Players must create space, track the football, secure possession, connect with support and continue contributing through repeated phases.

title: Shadow-Spoil Marking
primarySkill: Completing a mark while a shadow defender applies controlled spoil pressure

Organise players into groups of three.
Position the feeder eight to ten metres from the marker.
The marker begins with a defender one metre behind.
The defender follows the marker and extends one arm as shadow spoil pressure.
The defender may reach towards the football but may not make contact with the marker’s arms or body.
The feeder delivers controlled chest-height and overhead footballs.
Rotate roles after four to six repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The marker begins in a balanced position.
The defender starts directly behind or slightly to one side.
The feeder delivers the football towards the marker.
The marker tracks the football and presents the hands early.
The defender follows and performs a controlled shadow spoil.
The marker meets the football in front or at the highest comfortable point.
The football is cushioned and secured with two hands.
The marker moves it immediately to the protected side.
The defender stops pressure once possession is secured.
Players rotate through feeder, marker and defender roles.
coachingPoints: Track the football rather than watching the defender.
Position the body between the defender and the marking point.
Present the hands early.
Meet the football before it reaches the defender’s spoil zone.
Take overhead footballs at the highest comfortable point.
Maintain strong thumb position.
Secure the football with two hands.
Protect possession immediately after the mark.
Defenders must use controlled reach without contact.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the marker maintains focus on the football.
Whether body position protects the marking line.
Whether the hands are presented early.
Whether the football is met in front or overhead.
Whether the mark is secured despite pressure.
Whether the football moves to the protected side.
Whether the defender applies safe shadow pressure.

Include chest, overhead and low deliveries.
successIndicators: Meet the football before the spoil.
matchApplication: Most match marks involve some form of closing pressure. Learning to maintain focus and take the football before the defender reaches the contest helps players transfer unopposed technique into competitive situations.

title: Closing Defender Lead Mark
primarySkill: Completing a leading mark before a closing defender can spoil

groundSize: Lanes approximately eighteen metres long and seven metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced lead, closing-pressure and delivery management
setup:
Position the kicker at one end of the lane.
The marker begins twelve metres away.
The defender starts one to two metres behind the marker.
Mark a receiving gate four metres in front of the marker.
The defender may chase and attempt a controlled spoil at the football.
The defender may not push or contact the marker’s back.
A fourth player assists with rotation and football return.
Rotate all roles regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker secures possession and establishes visual connection.
The marker accelerates towards the receiving gate.
The defender chases from behind.
The kicker delivers into the marker’s forward path.
The marker tracks the football and extends both hands.
The player meets the football before the defender reaches the spoil point.
The defender attempts to contact the football only.
The marker secures and protects possession.
The repetition ends after the mark, spoil or clean recovery.
Players rotate roles.
coachingPoints: Lead when the kicker is ready.
Accelerate strongly through the first three steps.
Maintain a direct and balanced running line.
Present both hands before the football arrives.
Meet the football at full reach.
Avoid slowing early and allowing the defender to close.
Secure the football before turning.
Protect the football immediately after the mark.
Defenders must spoil the football rather than the player.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the lead begins from the kicker’s readiness.
Whether the marker creates separation.
Whether the kick is placed in front.
Whether the marker extends towards the football.
Whether the defender attempts a legal spoil.
Whether the marker slows unnecessarily.
Whether possession is secured and protected.

Add a second defender recovering from the side.
successIndicators: Complete the mark before the spoil.
matchApplication: A leading player must create separation and take the football before the trailing defender can spoil. Early hands and accurate delivery are critical when the closing space is limited.

title: Front-Position Contested Mark
primarySkill: Maintaining front position and completing a contested mark
objective: Develop the ability to establish and maintain front position between an opponent and the football before completing the mark.
groundSize: Contest lanes approximately twelve metres long and eight metres wide.
equipment: Optional bump pads for introductory body-position work
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced body-position and contest management
setup:
Organise players into groups of three.
Position the feeder eight to ten metres away.
The marker begins in front of the defender.
The defender starts within arm’s length behind.
The feeder delivers a controlled chest-height or slightly overhead football.
The defender may apply controlled body pressure and attempt a football-only spoil.
Pushing, holding and contact above the shoulders are prohibited.
Rotate roles after four repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The marker establishes front position.
The defender applies controlled pressure from behind.
The feeder delivers the football towards the contest.
The marker tracks the flight while maintaining the line.
The player widens the base and protects the marking space.
Both hands extend towards the football.
The defender attempts a controlled spoil.
The marker completes and secures the mark.
If the football spills, both players compete for the ground ball under controlled rules.
Players rotate roles.
coachingPoints: Establish front position before the football arrives.
Keep the feet active and the base balanced.
Use the body to protect space without holding or pushing.
Track the football continuously.
Meet the football in front or at the highest point.
Keep both hands strong.
Secure possession immediately.
Remain prepared to recover if the mark spills.
Defenders must contest the football legally.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the marker establishes front position.
Whether the base remains balanced.
Whether the player uses legal body positioning.
Whether the football is tracked under contact.
Whether the hands meet the football.
Whether the defender contests legally.
Whether both players react to a spill.

matchApplication: Front position gives a player the first opportunity to mark and forces the opponent to spoil from behind. Strong body positioning is central to contested marking across every area of the ground.

title: Side-by-Side Bodywork Mark
primarySkill: Maintaining marking balance during controlled side-by-side body contact
objective: Develop the ability to hold a legal side-by-side position, remain balanced and complete the mark while an opponent contests the same football.
groundSize: Contest lanes approximately fourteen metres long and eight metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced bodywork, safety and marking-balance management
setup:
Organise groups of three.
Position two marking players side by side inside a three-metre contest zone.
The feeder stands eight to ten metres away.
Players begin with light shoulder-to-shoulder contact.
The feeder delivers a controlled football above chest height.
Players may use legal body positioning but may not push, hold or extend an arm into the opponent.
The player who does not mark becomes the next feeder.
Alternate starting sides regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
Both players establish balanced side-by-side positions.
The feeder delivers the football towards the contest zone.
Players track the football while maintaining legal body contact.
Each player adjusts the feet towards the drop point.
Both attempt to mark the football at the highest comfortable point.
The successful player secures possession.
If the football spills, both players compete for the ground ball.
The winner exits through a nearby gate.
Players reset with starting sides reversed.
Rotate the feeder after each repetition.
coachingPoints: Maintain shoulder-to-shoulder contact rather than pushing.
Keep the feet active and the body balanced.
Track the football instead of staring at the opponent.
Move towards the drop point early.
Use the body to hold position legally.
Extend both hands towards the football.
Land or regain balance before protecting possession.
React immediately to spills.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players use legal shoulder-to-shoulder contact.
Whether feet remain active.
Whether players maintain vision of the football.
Whether one player gains better position.
Whether the marking attempt is balanced.
Whether contact remains controlled.
Whether spilled footballs are contested immediately.

successIndicators: Attempt the mark with two hands.
matchApplication: Many marking contests begin with players running or standing side by side. Legal body positioning and balance determine who reaches the football’s line and completes the mark.

title: High-Ball Mark Under Contact

The feeder delivers a controlled high football.
The defender applies controlled body contact before or during the jump but may not tunnel, push in the back or make contact above the shoulders.

Rotate roles after three to four repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers a high football towards the contest zone.
The marker and defender track the flight.
The marker establishes the preferred line to the drop point.
Controlled body contact occurs as both players prepare to jump.
The marker jumps vertically or slightly towards the football.
Both hands extend to the highest safe point.
The football is secured.
The player lands with bent knees and balanced feet.
The football is protected immediately after landing.
Players rotate roles.

Establish the drop point before jumping.
Maintain a strong core and balanced base.
Absorb legal contact without leaning dangerously.

Protect the football immediately.

title: Trailing-Defender Overhead Mark
primarySkill: Completing an overhead mark against a defender closing from behind
objective: Develop the ability to judge a higher kick, maintain front position and complete the overhead mark before a trailing defender can spoil.
groundSize: Lanes approximately twenty metres long and eight metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced high-flight, trailing-pressure and safety management

The defender starts one metre behind.
Mark a high-ball receiving zone in front of the marker.

The defender follows from behind.
The kicker delivers a higher football into the receiving zone.
The marker tracks the flight and adjusts speed.
The player maintains the front running line.

The marker reaches and completes the overhead mark.
The defender attempts a controlled spoil at the football.
The marker lands, secures and protects possession.
Players rotate roles.

Land in balance and protect possession.

title: Contested Mark and Ground-Ball Recovery
primarySkill: Competing for a mark and reacting immediately when the football spills
objective: Develop the ability to remain involved after an incomplete marking contest and win or pressure the resulting ground ball.
groundSize: Contest grids approximately twelve metres × ten metres with two exit gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced contest, recovery and transition management
setup:
Organise groups of four: feeder, two contesting players and one outside receiver.
Mark a central contest grid and two exit gates.
The feeder delivers a football that creates a realistic but safe marking contest.
Players compete legally for the mark.
If the football spills, the contest continues immediately at ground level.
The possession winner must connect with the outside receiver or exit through a gate.
Rotate roles regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers the football into the contest grid.
Both players establish position and attempt the mark.
If one player marks cleanly, the contest ends and the player exits through a gate.
If the football is spoiled or dropped, it remains live.
Both players regain balance and attack the ground ball.
The possession winner protects the football.
The player handballs to the outside receiver or carries through an exit gate.
The opponent applies controlled pressure.
The repetition ends after a clean exit or turnover.
Players rotate roles.
coachingPoints: Compete to mark the football with two hands.
Do not assume the mark will be completed.
Regain balance quickly after the aerial contest.
Locate the football immediately.
Use the body to protect the ground-ball line.
Keep the head over the football during collection.
Secure possession before releasing.
Apply pressure immediately when the opponent wins the football.
Maintain legal contact throughout both phases.

Whether players compete genuinely for the mark.

Whether both players react immediately to a spill.

title: Two-versus-One Marking Decision
primarySkill: Selecting and completing the best marking option in a two-versus-one contest
objective: Develop coordinated attacking movement and disposal choice when two marking options are opposed by one defender.
groundSize: Stations approximately twenty-five metres long and eighteen metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert option, defender and lead-coordination management
setup:
Position the kicker at one end of the station.
Place two markers at separate starting cones.
Mark one short lead gate and one deeper or wider lead gate.
Position one defender between the two markers.
Both markers may lead when the kicker gains possession.
The defender chooses which option to cover.
The kicker must select the clearer marking opportunity.
Rotate all roles regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker secures possession.
Both markers begin coordinated leads into separate lanes.
The defender moves to cover one option.
The kicker scans the defender’s position.
The football is delivered to the marker with the clearer advantage.
The selected marker competes for and completes the mark.
The unused marker becomes immediate post-mark support.
The defender attempts a legal spoil or interception.
Play continues briefly after the mark or turnover.
Players reset and rotate.
coachingPoints: The two markers must maintain different lanes and depths.
Both leads should be genuine.
The kicker should read the defender rather than predetermine the option.
Deliver to the player with the greatest positional advantage.

Whether markers create separate options.
Whether the defender is forced to choose.
Whether the kicker scans before disposal.
Whether the correct option is selected.
Whether delivery favours the marker.

Whether players react after turnover.

title: Pack-Entry Marking Contest
primarySkill: Entering a developing pack and competing for the football safely
objective: Develop the ability to judge when and how to enter a small pack marking contest without arriving too early, colliding dangerously or losing sight of the football.
groundSize: Contest areas approximately sixteen metres × fourteen metres.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert aerial safety, timing and multi-player contest management
setup:
Organise groups of five: feeder, two starting contest players, one pack-entry player and one outside receiver.
The two starting players establish controlled front and rear positions.
The pack-entry player begins four to six metres away.
The feeder delivers a controlled high football.
The pack-entry player may enter only after the football is kicked.
All players must avoid tunnelling, front-on contact and contact below the knees.
The outside receiver waits for the contest outcome.
Rotate roles regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The two starting players establish legal positions.
The feeder delivers a high football.
The pack-entry player reads the flight and approaches.
The player adjusts speed to arrive at the marking point rather than the bodies.
All players compete legally for the football.
A player completing the mark secures possession and connects with the outside receiver.
If the football spills, all players regain balance and contest the ground ball.
The possession winner exits the area.
The coach stops any unsafe approach or contact immediately.
Players reset and rotate roles.
coachingPoints: Track the football from the moment of delivery.
Enter the contest only when there is a realistic path to the football.
Adjust speed before reaching the pack.
Aim for the football’s drop point rather than running through opponents.
Jump vertically or towards the football.

title: Pressure and Contested Marking Assessment
primarySkill: Assessing marking technique and decision making under spoil, body and multi-player pressure
objective: Assess whether players can maintain safe, legal and effective marking technique across closing pressure, controlled contact and contested aerial situations.

coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert contested-marking assessment and safety management

Establish five assessment stations:
Station 1: Shadow and closing-defender marking.
Station 2: Front-position contested marking.
Station 3: Side-by-side and high-ball contact marking.
Station 4: Contested mark and ground-ball recovery.
Station 5: Two-versus-one and pack-entry marking decisions.
Divide players evenly between stations.
Assign a coach or trained observer to each station where possible.
Explain all legal contact, spoil and landing standards.
Allow one practice repetition before formal scoring.
Match players appropriately for size, age and physical capacity.
Stop any repetition that becomes unsafe.

Assess whether players continue tracking the football under pressure.
Record whether front or side position is established legally.
Observe hand presentation and high-point attempts.

successIndicators: Mark in front or at the high point.
matchApplication: Contested marking combines technical hands, body positioning, courage, judgement and second effort. This assessment identifies whether players can compete safely and effectively when opponents challenge the marking space.

title: One-on-One Drop-Zone Contest
primarySkill: Winning a live one-on-one marking contest at the football’s drop point

groundSize: Contest grids approximately sixteen metres × twelve metres with two exit gates.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert live-contest and safety management
setup:
Organise groups of three.

howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers the football into the live contest area.
Both players read the flight.

coachingPoints: Read the football before engaging the opponent.
Establish front, side or running position through legal movement.

Land safely and locate the football.

Maintain competitive intensity without unsafe contact.

Two contest players begin facing away from the feeder.

Mark a drop zone eight to twelve metres behind them.
The coach gives a turn signal as the feeder delivers a high football.
Both players turn, locate and compete for the mark.
Contact is controlled and all spoil actions must target the football.
A fourth player assists with return and rotation.

Both contest players begin facing the coach.
The coach gives the turn signal.
The feeder delivers a high football into the contest area.
Players turn over the most efficient shoulder and locate the ball.

The advantaged player attempts to mark.
The other player attempts a legal spoil.

Players reset and rotate roles.
coachingPoints: Turn through the hips and feet.
Locate the football before engaging the opponent.
Accelerate to the drop point.
Adjust speed as the flight becomes clear.
Use legal body position.

Players communicate who will attack the mark, spoil or remain at ground level.
Normal legal marking contact applies.
Rotate the feeder and starting positions.

The opposition applies pressure and attempts a turnover.
Reset and rotate roles.

Avoid teammates competing against each other unnecessarily.

Use legal body positioning.
Mark with two hands when possible.
Defenders should spoil towards teammate support.
Maintain balance on landing.
Transition immediately to ground level.
Finish the possession through the exit gate.

Whether teams communicate roles.
Whether teammates avoid aerial collisions.

title: Three-Player Pack Mark and Exit

The single opponent competes for the mark or spoil.
Rotate the numerical roles regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers a high football into the pack area.
All players track the flight.
The two-player team communicates who attacks the football.
The supporting teammate positions for the spill.
The opponent competes to mark or spoil.
A completed mark is secured and released to the outside receiver.
If the football spills, all players compete at ground level.
The possession winner exits through a nominated gate.
Pressure continues until the football leaves the contest area.
Players rotate roles and numerical advantage.
coachingPoints: Avoid both teammates attacking the same football without communication.

The supporting player must position for likely spoil direction.
The outnumbered player should use body position and spoil strategically.
Maintain safe approach and landing lines.
Secure the football before disposal.

Continue the contest after any spill.
Apply pressure until the exit is complete.

title: Repeat Aerial Contest
primarySkill: Maintaining marking and recovery quality across repeated aerial contests

Position one feeder outside each zone.

The coach controls the timing and delivery of each football.
Complete blocks of four to six contests.
Match players appropriately.
Provide planned recovery between blocks.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers the first football into Zone A.
Players compete for the mark or spoil.

The second feeder delivers the next football.
Players reorganise aerial and ground-level roles.
The contest continues through mark, spoil and recovery.
Players return towards Zone A for the next repetition.
Complete four to six alternating contests.
Recover, review one technical priority and repeat.
coachingPoints: Reorganise roles before every delivery.
Continue tracking the football under fatigue.
Maintain two-hand marking attempts.
Avoid jumping when the body is not safely positioned.
Land with bent knees.
Recover immediately after each contest.
Communicate who attacks the football.
Technique and safety take priority over completing the full block.
Stop if contact or landing quality deteriorates.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether roles are reorganised.
Whether football tracking declines.
Whether players jump from safe positions.
Whether hands and marking technique remain strong.
Whether landings remain controlled.
Whether second effort is immediate.

matchApplication: Players may face several aerial contests within a short period. The ability to reset roles and maintain safe technique under fatigue is essential late in quarters and during repeat entries.

title: Intercept Mark Under Forward Pressure
primarySkill: Completing an intercept mark while opposition forwards apply closing pressure
objective: Develop a defender’s ability to leave an opponent or zone, attack the football’s line and secure an intercept mark before transitioning possession out of defence.

Position one attacking ball carrier outside the defensive area.

Position one direct defender with each forward.
Add one intercept defender starting between or behind the lanes.
Mark two defensive exit gates.
The ball carrier attempts to kick to one forward.
The intercept defender reads the delivery and decides whether to leave the starting position.
Controlled forward pressure continues after the mark.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking ball carrier scans both forwards.

The intercept defender reads the flight and movement.

The defender secures and protects possession.
The defensive team exits through a gate by handball or kick.
If the football is spoiled or dropped, play remains live.
coachingPoints: Maintain awareness of both the football and direct opponents.

title: Complete Congestion and Contested Marking Assessment
primarySkill: Assessing marking performance under body pressure, congestion, repeated effort and live aerial competition
objective: Assess each player’s ability to track, position, mark, spoil, recover and transition across demanding contested-marking situations.
groundSize: Six assessment stations arranged across half a ground.

coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert assessment, contact and workload management

Station 5: Repeat aerial contests.

Divide players evenly between stations.
Match players appropriately for physical size and capacity.
Assign trained coaches or observers.
Explain legal contact, spoil, jump and landing standards.
Allow one practice repetition before formal scoring.
Schedule recovery before repeated and pack-contest stations.
Stop any unsafe repetition immediately.

At Station 1, each player completes four drop-zone positioning contests.
At Station 2, each player completes four leading marks with controlled late pressure.
At Station 3, players complete four live one-on-one contests from varied starting positions.
At Station 4, players rotate through aerial, support and defensive pack roles.
At Station 5, players complete one block of four to six repeat aerial contests.
At Station 6, defenders complete four intercept decisions followed by rebound exits.
Observers score flight judgement, position, hand presentation, mark-or-spoil choice and security.

Assess football tracking before and during body pressure.

matchApplication: Contested marking requires technical skill, body positioning, decision making, courage and repeated effort. This assessment determines whether players can compete safely and effectively when the football, opponents and support roles are all live.

title: Defensive Exit Marking Triangle
primarySkill: Using angled marking options to exit defensive 50

Position Player A near the goal square or defensive pocket with the football.
Position Player B as a short angled option.
Position Player C wider and slightly forward.
Position Player D beyond the first defensive line.
Mark three receiving gates that form a triangle away from goal.
Place additional players behind each position for rotation.
Players follow their disposal into the next position.
Mirror the pattern on both sides of defensive 50.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player B begins a short angled lead away from the goal square.

title: Corridor Marking Connection

Player A gains possession in midfield.

title: Behind-the-Football Marking Reset
primarySkill: Using a marking option behind the football to retain possession and change the attacking angle

groundSize: A possession area approximately thirty-five metres long and thirty metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert risk, patience and support management
setup:
Position Player A with the football in the centre or wing area.
Position two forward marking options.

title: Full-Ground Marking Transition Pattern

Players lead, mark and connect into the next positional zone.
Previous disposers maintain support behind.
Begin with one football before adding additional waves.

title: Team Marking Movement Assessment

title: Centre Clearance Marking Chain

title: Defensive Switch Marking Decision

title: Width-and-Depth Marking Possession
primarySkill: Maintaining team width and depth during marking possession

title: Numerical-Deficit Marking Retention

howTheDrillWorks:
In Phase 1, players complete chest, overhead, low and one-grab marking assessments.
In Phase 2, players complete straight, angled, lateral, double and backward-flight marking tasks.
In Phase 3, players rotate through front-position, side-by-side, high-ball and ground-recovery contests.
In Phase 4, players complete intercept, fly-or-stay, spare-defender and position-specific marking scenarios.
In Phase 5, teams execute defensive exits, switches, midfield connections and forward marking patterns.
In Phase 6, teams complete a live scoreboard or game-plan simulation.
Coaches score tracking, footwork, hand position, security, contact management, movement and tactical selection.
Players receive one technical strength, one tactical strength and two priority actions.
Groups repeat one selected task linked to their most important development need.
Finish with a player and coach review of the complete marking chapter.
